questions.stem: Describe planning.
options: Deciding in advance what to do, how, when and who
Working harder and longer whenever problems appear in the business
Writing a detailed report after the work is done to explain what happened
Telling staff to follow their instincts and deal with each situation as it comes
questions.why: Planning converts 'whatever happens, happens' into 'if X happens, we do Y'. It is the first function because the other three need a plan to serve. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Explain why planning is called the first function of management.
options: Organising, leading and controlling all need a plan to serve
It is the easiest function to do
Managers are paid to plan, not to act, so planning takes most of their time
It was invented first, in 1916, before the other functions had names
questions.why: The plan gives the other functions their direction. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Explain the saying 'plans are nothing; planning is everything'.
options: Plans change when reality surprises, but a team that planned can adjust quickly instead of panicking
Written plans are useless, so managers should spend their time acting rather than writing
Only the planning department matters; the rest of the organisation simply follows its instructions
Plans never change once they are written, so the planning stage must be done perfectly
questions.why: The thinking survives even when the plan changes. See the answer to questions 1 and 2 in §4.1.

questions.stem: Differentiate mission, vision and goals.
options: Mission = why we exist; vision = where we are going; goals = what we will achieve, with numbers and dates
Mission = the numbers we must hit; vision = the daily tasks; goals = the company's history and values
Mission = where we are going; vision = why we exist; goals = the slogan and the logo
All three mean the same thing, and companies choose whichever word sounds best to customers
questions.why: The mission explains the vision, the vision inspires the goals, the goals drive daily work. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Identify the three levels of planning with their time horizons.
options: Strategic — years; tactical — months; operational — days and weeks
Strategic — days and weeks; tactical — years; operational — months
Operational — years; strategic — days and weeks; tactical — months
Top — hours; middle — days and weeks; frontline — years
questions.why: Three levels of planning match three levels of manager: top (years), middle (months), frontline (days). See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the five parts of a SMART goal.
options: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Simple, Modern, Ambitious, Rapid, Tested
Strategic, Managed, Approved, Reported, Tracked
Short, Meaningful, Affordable, Realistic, Timed
questions.why: SMART is the quality test for a goal: the upgrade always adds a number, a date and a how. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four boxes of a SWOT analysis.
options: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
Sales, Workers, Orders, Taxes
Strategy, Work, Output, Time
Suppliers, Wages, Owners, Technology
questions.why: Inside: strengths and weaknesses. Outside: opportunities and threats. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Explain why plans fail, according to the chapter.
options: Uncertainty without a Plan B, poor communication, lack of commitment and unrealistic goals
Too many meetings, too many reports and too many people involved in the planning
Managers planning too far ahead when the business should concentrate on this month
Teams working too hard on the plan and too little on the daily work that pays the wages
questions.why: Four reasons plans fail; impossible targets teach teams that targets are decoration. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Identify the six steps of decision-making in order.
options: Identify the problem → gather information → generate alternatives → evaluate options → choose and act → evaluate results
Choose and act → gather information → identify the problem → evaluate results → generate alternatives → evaluate options
Generate alternatives → choose and act → identify the problem → gather information → evaluate options → evaluate results
Gather information → choose and act → identify the problem → generate alternatives → evaluate options → evaluate results
questions.why: Decide the real problem first; solutions after. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Explain why 'sales dropping' is not the real problem in step 1.
options: It is a symptom — WHY sales drop is the problem
Sales never matter to managers, who should concentrate on costs and quality instead
Step 1 is about choosing a solution, and dropping sales do not point to any particular one
Dropping sales are always caused by staff, so the problem is a people problem
questions.why: The real problem is the cause behind the symptom; almost everyone jumps to solutions. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Differentiate rational from intuitive decisions.
options: Rational uses data and the six steps in full; intuitive uses fast pattern-recognition built from experience
Rational decisions are always wrong because they are slow; intuitive decisions are always right because they are fast
Rational is for small decisions that do not matter; intuitive is for the big decisions that shape the business
They are the same thing with different names, and the chapter uses whichever word fits the sentence
questions.why: Both are real ways to decide; the mistake is using the wrong engine for the situation. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four bias traps described in the chapter.
options: Overconfidence, emotional decisions, groupthink, confirmation bias
Laziness, greed, anger and fear of the boss
Planning, organising, leading and controlling
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
questions.why: Every brain falls into them; the more senior and confident the manager, the more dangerous. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Describe groupthink.
options: Everyone privately doubts but nobody speaks, so the group agrees its way off a cliff
A group that argues so much about every option that it cannot reach a decision in time
A group that thinks faster than one person
Deciding only with people who already share your opinion so that the meeting is short
questions.why: Silence is read as agreement. The fix: collect written views before the meeting, ask the most junior first, appoint a devil's advocate. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's rule on AI in decision-making.
options: AI is an adviser, not a judge — the manager stays accountable
AI should make all routine decisions because it has no emotions and no bias
AI should never be used by managers because it does not know the company's mission
AI decides, and the manager's job is to explain the decision to customers and staff
questions.why: AI learns from past data, optimises the number it is given and does not know your mission or ethics; 'the AI decided' satisfies no customer, court or team. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Explain when a manager should decide together with the team rather than alone.
options: When the problem is complex, commitment matters, or the team knows things the manager cannot
When speed is critical and the decision has to be made in the next few minutes
When accountability is clearly the manager's and nobody else will be blamed
When the group adds no new information but wants to feel involved in the decision
questions.why: Alone for speed and clear accountability; together for complexity and commitment. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Select the goal that passes all five SMART tests.
options: Raise weekday sales from 240 to 300 cups a day within 8 weeks by launching a morning combo and a loyalty card
Improve sales significantly over the coming months by serving customers better than any competitor
Become the best café in the UAE someday, known for quality, service and a loyal community
Work harder every day, open earlier, close later and make sure every customer leaves happy
questions.why: The strong version adds a number, a date and a how. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the goal 'Improve customer satisfaction'. Determine the SMART test it fails most clearly.
options: Measurable — there is no number to know if you reached it
Relevant — it does not serve the mission of a café, which is to sell coffee
Achievable — it is impossible to improve satisfaction once customers have formed an opinion
Specific — it names the customers but not the staff who will serve them
questions.why: 'Improve' is a wish; a number — such as 'by 20% this semester' — makes it measurable. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Classify the plan 'Standardise recipes this year so a second branch can copy them'.
options: Tactical — months, middle managers
Strategic — years, top managers
Operational — days, frontline managers
A mission statement
questions.why: Department-level plans over months are tactical. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Determine the SWOT pair behind the move 'use our location to own the morning rush before anyone opens'.
options: Strength + Opportunity — the attack move
Weakness + Threat — the defence move
Strength + Threat — the holding move
Weakness + Opportunity — the repair move
questions.why: S + O is the attack move; W + T is the defence move. Pairing the boxes is planning. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Determine the SWOT pair behind the move 'find a second coffee supplier before the chain arrives'.
options: Weakness + Threat — the defence move
Strength + Opportunity — the attack move
Strength + Weakness
Opportunity + Threat
questions.why: One supplier is a weakness; the chain opening is a threat. W + T defends. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a student whose study plan said 'six hours a day' and who gave up in week two. Determine the planning barrier.
options: Unrealistic goals
Poor communication
Uncertainty with no Plan B
Lack of resources
questions.why: Impossible targets teach people that targets are decoration. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Analyse the café owner who must choose ONE of: reduce prices, improve quality, increase marketing, fire staff — before knowing why sales dropped. Determine the mistake.
options: Jumping to step 5 (choose) before step 1 (identify the real problem)
Choosing too few alternatives — four options are not enough for a decision this important
Gathering too much information — the owner should act before the sales fall further
Involving the team too early — the owner should decide alone and then inform the staff
questions.why: A, B, C and D were all step-5 answers to a step-1 question. See the answer to question 3 in §4.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the Bad Reviews case: 50-minute waits, wrong orders, exhausted staff. Determine the most likely real problem.
options: Understaffing or poor organisation at peak hours — the three complaints share one cause
Customers who are too demanding and leave reviews after a single bad experience
A bad online review website that attracts complaints and hides the positive comments
Prices that are too high for the quality, so customers expect more than the café delivers
questions.why: Step 1: look at what the complaints have in common; the rating is the symptom. See Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the right step-2 action for the student event nobody attended.
options: Ask twenty students who did NOT come, and check when and where it was announced
Book a bigger hall for next time so that more students feel the event is important
Cancel all future events until the student club can show it has enough members
Ask the student club president to explain the failure and propose a new event
questions.why: Gather information before opinions harden — from the people who did not come. See the sample in §4.5.

questions.stem: Compare a veteran chef who 'knows' a dish is wrong before tasting it with a first-year manager whose gut says 'fire the new employee'. Determine the chapter's advice.
options: Trust the chef's experienced intuition in a familiar situation; distrust the first-year manager's gut — it has not earned trust yet
Trust both — intuition is always right, because it comes from a deeper part of the mind than analysis
Trust neither — only data counts, and both the chef and the manager should wait for the numbers
Trust the first-year manager because the decision is urgent, and trust the chef only after tasting the dish
questions.why: Experienced intuition is compressed data; in new situations 'gut feeling' is just bias wearing confidence. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Select the right engine for choosing a new coffee supplier when there is time and data.
options: Rational — data, analysis, the six steps in full
Intuitive — go with the first supplier you like, because first impressions are usually right
Emotional — choose the friendliest salesperson, because the relationship will matter later
Collective — let the team vote without information so that everyone feels committed
questions.why: High stakes, time available, data available → rational. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify the bias trap when a manager says 'I know this market — no need to check'.
options: Overconfidence
Groupthink
Confirmation bias
Emotional decision
questions.why: Experience earns a hypothesis, not a verdict; the fix is one independent check above a money threshold. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Select the rule that prevents a manager from firing someone in a moment of fury.
options: The 24-hour rule — no irreversible people decisions while angry
Ask 'we all agree, yes?' before acting so that the team shares responsibility
Look for evidence that supports the firing so that the decision can be defended later
Decide faster so that the anger does not grow and the decision is made with a clear head
questions.why: The emotion fades; the decision stays. See the emotional-decisions trap in §4.7.

questions.stem: Identify the bias trap when a team only looks for evidence that supports the idea it already likes.
options: Confirmation bias
Overconfidence
Groupthink
Emotional decision
questions.why: The favourite trap of smart people; the fix is to ask for the strongest evidence AGAINST. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who uses AI forecasting to predict the Iftar rush by hour but checks the plan against the restaurant's values and staff. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Correct — AI as adviser for patterns and volume, with the manager accountable for judgement
Wrong — the manager should follow the AI exactly, because it has seen more Iftar seasons than any manager
Wrong — AI should not be used in restaurants at all
Correct only if the AI also decides the staffing, so that the forecast and the rota cannot disagree
questions.why: AI is strongest where humans are weakest (patterns, volume) and weakest where humans are strongest (ethics, judgement in new situations). See §4.8.

questions.stem: Explain what a plan changes in a team's thinking.
options: It turns 'whatever happens, happens' into 'if X happens, we do Y'
It makes work faster automatically, because everyone knows what to do without asking
It removes the need for leading, because a good plan motivates people by itself
It guarantees success as long as the team follows the plan exactly as written
questions.why: Planning converts luck into if-then thinking. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe a mission statement.
options: A short statement of why the organisation exists
A list of this year's numbers
A description of where the company will be in ten years
The company's daily schedule
questions.why: Mission = why we exist. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe a vision statement.
options: A picture of where the organisation is going
The reason the company exists today and the needs it serves
A goal with a number and a date that the team must reach
A goal with a number and a date
questions.why: Vision = where we are going; it inspires the goals. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Explain how mission, vision and goals connect.
options: The mission explains the vision, the vision inspires the goals, the goals drive daily work
They are three names for the same thing, chosen to suit different audiences
Goals come first, then the mission, then the vision is written to match them
Only the vision matters; the mission and the goals are paperwork for the annual report
questions.why: Each level feeds the next. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe strategic planning.
options: Long-term direction set by top managers, thinking in years
Daily schedules set by frontline managers, thinking in days and weeks
Department plans set by middle managers over the coming months
A list of today's tasks for each employee
questions.why: Strategic = years, top managers. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Explain what 'Time-bound' adds to a goal.
options: A date by which the goal must be reached
A number that makes the goal measurable
A reason why the goal matters to the mission
A person who is responsible for reaching the goal
questions.why: The T in SMART is the deadline. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Describe an opportunity in SWOT.
options: An outside condition the organisation could use to its advantage
An inside strength that the organisation has built up over time
An inside weakness that the organisation needs to repair
An outside danger that could damage the organisation
questions.why: Opportunities and threats are outside; strengths and weaknesses are inside. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Explain the 'attack move' and the 'defence move' in SWOT.
options: Attack pairs a strength with an opportunity; defence pairs a weakness with a threat
Attack means lowering prices to win customers; defence means raising them to protect profit
Attack is the strategy for big firms; defence is the strategy for small ones
Both mean copying what competitors do, either before them or after them
questions.why: S + O attacks; W + T defends. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Describe step 3 of the decision process.
options: Generate alternatives — list several possible solutions before judging any
Choose the first solution that appears and act on it before the problem grows
Evaluate the results of last year's decision to see whether it worked
Gather information about the symptom from customers and staff
questions.why: Step 3 creates options; step 4 evaluates them. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Explain why step 6, evaluate results, matters.
options: It tells you whether the decision worked and feeds the next decision
It is only paperwork for the audit file
It replaces step 1, because evaluating results shows what the next problem will be
It makes the decision final, so that nobody can reopen the question afterwards
questions.why: Evaluate results closes the loop. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe when intuitive decisions are safe to trust.
options: When the decider has long experience in a familiar situation
Always — gut feeling is never wrong, because it comes from a deeper part of the mind
Never — only data counts, and feelings should be kept out of management decisions
Only for new managers, who have not yet learned to analyse decisions properly
questions.why: Experienced intuition is compressed data; new-situation gut feeling is bias. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter calls experienced intuition 'compressed data'.
options: Years of seeing patterns let the expert recognise the answer fast without conscious analysis
Experts keep spreadsheets in their heads and run the numbers faster than other people
Intuition is random, but experts are lucky more often because they decide more often
Experts never think consciously about decisions, so their answers come from memory alone
questions.why: Pattern recognition built from experience. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify the situation where the rational engine is the right choice.
options: High stakes, time available, data available
An emergency with seconds to decide and no time to gather data
A familiar daily choice that the manager has made hundreds of times
A decision nobody cares about, where the outcome makes no difference
questions.why: Rational for high stakes with time and data. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Describe the fix for overconfidence.
options: One independent check above a money threshold
Decide faster so that doubt does not creep in
Ask only people who agree, so that confidence stays high
Avoid data, because it only confirms what experience already knows
questions.why: Experience earns a hypothesis, not a verdict. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Describe the fix for groupthink.
options: Collect written views before the meeting, ask the most junior first, appoint a devil's advocate
Let the boss speak first so that everyone knows which direction the discussion is taking
Vote quickly to save time, because long discussions make groups less decisive
Keep meetings short and limit them to the three most senior people in the room
questions.why: These three steps stop silence being read as agreement. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Describe what AI is good at in decision-making.
options: Patterns, volume and speed in past data
Knowing the company's mission and ethics
Judging a situation it has never seen
Taking accountability
questions.why: AI is strongest where humans are weakest, and weakest where humans are strongest. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Explain when a manager should decide alone.
options: When speed is critical and accountability is clearly the manager's
When the problem is complex and has many possible causes
When commitment from the team matters most for the plan to work
When the team knows more about the problem than the manager does
questions.why: Alone for speed and clear accountability. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Classify the plan 'Open a second branch in Sharjah within three years'.
options: Strategic
Tactical
Operational
A mission statement
questions.why: Years and direction = strategic. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Determine the SWOT box for 'a new coffee chain opens next door next month'.
options: Threat
Weakness
Weak point
Opportunity
questions.why: Outside and dangerous = threat. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Determine the step a manager skipped when she offered discounts before checking why customers left.
options: Step 1 — identify the real problem
Step 4 — evaluate options
Step 5 — choose and act
Step 6 — evaluate results
questions.why: She acted on a symptom without finding the cause. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Classify a veteran pilot who decides in two seconds during an emergency.
options: Intuitive decision from experience — the right engine for the situation
Rational decision — the pilot ran through the six steps very quickly
Emotional decision — the pilot reacted to fear rather than to the facts
Groupthink — the pilot did what the rest of the crew expected
questions.why: Familiar situation, no time: experienced intuition fits. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Select the decision that needs the rational engine.
options: Choosing a supplier for a three-year contract
Picking a colour for today's poster in the staff room
A chef tasting a sauce and deciding whether it needs salt
Deciding where to have lunch with a colleague
questions.why: High stakes and time available → rational. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Classify a meeting where everyone privately disagrees but nobody speaks.
options: Groupthink
Overconfidence
Confirmation bias
Rational decision-making
questions.why: Silence read as agreement is groupthink. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's position on a hotel that lets AI set room prices with no human review.
options: AI may advise, but a human must own and check the decision
Fully acceptable — AI has no bias and prices rooms more accurately than any manager
AI should never touch prices, because pricing is the heart of the hotel's strategy
The guests should decide prices through an auction, with the AI running the bidding
questions.why: AI is an adviser, not a judge. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Select the decision that should be made together with the team.
options: Redesigning a workflow the team knows better than the manager
Evacuating the building during a fire alarm
Signing today's delivery note from the regular supplier
Choosing the manager's own desk and chair for the office
questions.why: Together when the team knows things the manager cannot. See §4.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says 'the AI decided' when a customer complains. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Unacceptable — the manager stays accountable for decisions AI only advised
Acceptable — the AI is responsible for its decision
Acceptable if the AI was expensive, because the company has invested in its judgement
The customer should ask the AI to explain itself, since it knows why it decided
questions.why: 'The AI decided' satisfies no customer, court or team. See §4.8.
